new_statements.quote: Words are stressed on the penultimate syllable. High vowels, especially /i/, are often elided word finally, so that [...'CVCi#] sequences become [...'CVC#], with final stress. Subject prefixes can not be stressed. There are several particles (e.g. /-ŋa/ 'only, just'; /-ŋi/ completive) which cliticise to preceding words and shift their stress to the right.
new_statements.citation: Early, Robert. 2002. Lamen. In John Lynch, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley (eds), The Oceanic Languages, 671-680. Richmond: Curzon.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. Surface final stress arises when a word-final high vowel (especially /i/) is elided after stress assignment. Subject-marking prefixes never carry stress, and enclitic particles such as -ŋa 'only' and -ŋi (completive) count as part of the word and move the stress one position rightward.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress on words whose final high vowel has been elided; subject prefixes unstressable; stress shifts right when clitic particles attach. Also p. 671: in ['ŋ.ka] 'yes' the nasal component of /ŋg/ is an initial stressed syllabic nasal.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word; the sketch treats prefix+root and root+clitic complexes as the stress domain (prefixes excluded from bearing stress, enclitics included). No phrase-level statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Early 2002 describes the language of Lamen (Lamenu) Island off NW Epi, exactly lame1260 (ISO lmu); Early 1994 and Lynch & Crowley 2001 note that speakers also call it 'Lewo', but it is distinct from Lewo proper (lewo1242) on Epi mainland. No dialect subdivision is described.

sources.note: Describes Lewo (lewo1242), the closest relative, not Lamen: §3.4 Stress gives Lewo penultimate stress with final-syllable extrametricality and alternating secondary stress. §2.2.4.2 'Lewo and Lamen' discusses the language boundary and lexical differences only; no Lamen stress statement.
